rewrites.summary:
For a trans visitor to Tlaxcala, the operative facts are documents and the legal floor: an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition exists via the state's 2019 reform of the Civil Code (Decree D.113, dated 1 October 2019), with no court proceeding; the national Supreme Court's 17 October 2018 ruling makes name and gender-marker change available through a simple administrative procedure based on self-declaration; and same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since the final states completed legalisation in 2022.

No jurisdiction-specific ordinance, incident series or enforcement pattern targeting transgender people appears in the surviving sources; Mexico's national criminal law and gender-recognition regime apply here as elsewhere in the country. A March 2025 count by Human Rights Watch places the jurisdiction among the 22 of 32 state units that have legislated a gender-recognition procedure — not among the six that have enacted none.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Parent-country context: Human Rights Watch's March 2025 state-by-state feature counts 22 of 32 Mexican states with a legislated gender-recognition procedure and lists the six without one, contrasting this jurisdiction's position with states such as Tabasco and Tamaulipas that lack a procedure — comparison units, not local findings.

The national armed forces' documented severe harassment of outed LGBTQ soldiers, often ending in discharge, is parent-country context with marginal practical exposure for a visitor.

rewrites.summary:
For a trans visitor to Yucatán the operative document fact is recent: the state's 2024 reform of the Civil Registry Law (publication in the official gazette on 26 April 2024) created an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition, placing the jurisdiction among Mexican state units that offer an administrative — rather than court-ordered — route to update legal gender on documents. Human Rights Watch's March 2025 count likewise places it among the 22 of 32 states with a legislated procedure, not among the six without one.

Marriage equality is settled: same-sex marriage was secured through court rulings from July 2013 and codified by the state's September 2021 constitutional amendment and 1 March 2022 secondary legislation; a conversion-therapy (ECOSIG) ban has been in effect since 25 August 2021. No jurisdiction-specific ordinance, incident series or enforcement pattern against transgender people is supported by the surviving sources; the national criminal and human-rights framework applies in the state as elsewhere in Mexico.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Litigation flux, now resolved: the Third District Court ruled on 1 July 2013 that two petitioners were able to marry; the state's first same-sex wedding followed on 8 August 2013; the state Constitutional Court dismissed a challenge to the Civil Code's marriage provisions on 2 March 2015 and the national Supreme Court dismissed the appeal on 31 May 2015.

Parent-country legal history, not local risk: same-sex acts were decriminalised nationally as early as 1871, and the national conversion-therapy ban passed the lower chamber of the national legislature in March 2023 (267-104) after a 69-16 vote in the upper chamber in October 2022 — parent-country policy context that the local 2021 ECOSIG enactment sits within.

rewrites.summary:
For a trans visitor to Zacatecas the document route is recent and explicit: a December 2022 reform of the state's Family Code — approved by the 64th Legislature with 14 votes in favour and 7 against — establishes the possibility of issuing a new birth certificate recognising an applicant's gender identity, principally for the trans community, and Human Rights Watch's March 2025 feature records the same reform as an administrative procedure, with the Civil Registry director's 2023 implementing guidelines.

A protective criminal-law floor applies: since 25 August 2021 the state Penal Code prohibits and sanctions conversion therapies, penalising incitement to hatred or violence on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression with one to three years' imprisonment or community work, and the same session typified hate crimes motivated by sexual orientation and gender identity. The jurisdiction is not among the six Mexican state units without a legislated gender-recognition procedure per Human Rights Watch's March 2025 count (22 of 32). No jurisdiction-specific ordinance, incident series or enforcement pattern targeting transgender people appears in the surviving sources; the national criminal law and gender-recognition regime apply here as elsewhere in the country.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Legislative flux inside the jurisdiction, now settled: the gender-identity law initiative debated alongside the conversion-therapy ban in August 2021 failed to obtain enough votes at the time — the ban passed while the reform remained pending — and the reform only passed in December 2022. The current legal floor is therefore recent; no neighbour comparison finding beyond the national 22-of-32 count appears in the sources.
rewrites.localsOnly: Resident-facing law: the Family Code reform is the resident birth-register route — a new birth certificate recognising an applicant's gender identity, principally for the trans community — enacted by the state's own legislature. No resident discrimination data or local surveys for the jurisdiction appear in the surviving sources.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: The Human Rights Watch overview page for 31 March 2025 was not retrievable at fetch time; its 22-of-32 count is carried via the claim note. The La Jornada Zacatecas press report was verified through an archived Wayback Machine snapshot of 7 October 2025 because the live URL is Cloudflare-blocked (HTTP 403); the live page could not be read directly. The absence of a local hostile incident series or enforcement pattern is noted, not proof of none.

rewrites.summary:
For a trans visitor to Newfoundland and Labrador the local legal floor is quiet: no jurisdiction-specific trans law, enforcement pattern or official statement was found; criminal law and the national human-rights framework apply uniformly, and the jurisdiction has no facility or expression rule differing from the national position. The documented risk signals are weak — police-reported hate crime is the lowest in the country (5.3 per 100,000 in 2024) — and risk is assessed at parity with the national picture.

Documents: the province's sex-designation change requires birth in the province or three months' residence, operates without any surgery requirement and without an application fee, and the province states it cannot guarantee that an 'X' gender marker on its documents will be accepted by authorities in other organisations — the caveat that matters for a visitor carrying provincial records while travelling; the 2016 amendment also removed the surgery requirement for changing the gender marker on a birth or marriage registration.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Parent-nation context: the national police-reported hate-crime series shows 4,882 reported incidents nationally (+1% on 2023) at a national rate of 12.1 per 100,000, with this jurisdiction's 5.3 the joint-lowest provincial rate, tied with one other province, against a highest provincial rate of 16.0 elsewhere; federal criminal law and the federal human-rights framework apply uniformly as the operative floor.
rewrites.localsOnly:
Resident data: police-reported hate crime in the province was the joint-lowest in the country at 5.3 per 100,000 in 2024, alongside one other province; the +51% rise that year came from 19 to 29 reported incidents — very small absolute numbers, so the rate change is statistically fragile.

Resident legal history: the 2016 amendment (Royal Assent 13 April 2016) removed the surgery requirement, bringing provincial law into compliance with an order of a Board of Inquiry under the provincial Human Rights Commission (the December 2015 ruling on complaints from two trans women); the 2021 amendment (Royal Assent 23 June 2021) extended the route to people born outside the province after three months' residence, with the change certificate priced at $25, counting as official provincial identification that could be leveraged by the applicant to update records in other jurisdictions; applicants must be 16 or older, or represented by a parent or legal guardian for under-16s (with written consent of individuals aged 12 to 15).
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
The province's low overall hate-crime rate and its 2024 percentage rise cover all motivations (race, religion, sexual orientation) from tiny absolute counts; neither is a trans-specific signal.

The 2021 government release priced the change certificate at $25 while the current official page states no application fee, with charges only for official copies of updated documents — a fee discrepancy the sources do not reconcile. The Egale analysis page by an LGBTIQ+ organisation was not retrievable at fetch time and is carried via its claim note. The province's own statement that it cannot guarantee acceptance of its 'X' marker elsewhere is the government's caveat, not third-party evidence of how other jurisdictions treat provincial documents.

rewrites.summary:
For a trans visitor to Prince Edward Island the legal floor is quiet: no jurisdiction-specific trans law, incident pattern, official statement or rate deviation was found; federal criminal law and human-rights protection apply uniformly, and the jurisdiction has no facility, expression or registration rule differing from the national position. Risk assessed at parity with the national picture; no systematic count of trans deaths exists to measure outcomes here specifically.

Documents: gender-marker change on provincial documents works through self-declared gender with a physician's letter and no surgery requirement (since the April 2016 amendment), and since December 2018 provincial photo ID — including driver's licences — can carry an 'X' or blank gender marker, the first such blank option offered anywhere in the country; adults need birth in the jurisdiction plus three months' residence, with physician attestation and signature formalities.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Parent-nation context: the national police-reported hate-crime release records 4,882 reported incidents in 2024 (+1% on 2023) and a national rate of 12.1 per 100,000, giving no jurisdiction-specific rate or incident count for the province — the parity finding rests on that absence, alongside eight provincial units recording stable or declining rates nationally.
rewrites.localsOnly:
Resident data: the national release gives no jurisdiction-specific rate or incident count — the parity finding is supported by that absence. The 2016 reporting states the provincial health body would cover the costs of three surgeries for transgender patients.

Resident document regime: adults must be born in the province and resident there for at least three months (minors under 18 may apply through a legal custodian, with written consent of any other custodian or parent and of the child if aged 12 or older); the application requires a physician statement, a written statement by the applicant, and a signature before a commissioner of oaths at the Vital Statistics office. The resident advocacy community welcomed the 2016 change because surgery is expensive and the closest provider was outside the province, and called for a future third gender category.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: An analysis page by an LGBTIQ+ organisation was not retrievable at fetch time (redirect to a stub); the live provincial information page is bot-gated and its content comes from an archived Wayback Machine snapshot of 1 July 2022. No source covers border or airport screening procedures for entering travellers, passport or identity-document policy at the national level, marriage, or partner-travel with the jurisdiction; those remain unverified for this jurisdiction. The claim that the blank gender option was the first offered in the country is the province's own release, and the physician's-letter requirement is stated but its enforcement in practice is not documented.

rewrites.summary:

The capital hosts a large, organised 2SLGBTQ+ community with institutional support, while the documented national hostility pattern elsewhere concentrates in other provinces' school-board and library politics — not this jurisdiction. rewrites.summary:
For a trans visitor to Quebec the recorded risk profile rests on the national data series: the March 2026 release on police-reported hate crime (2024 data) shows gender-identity/expression-motivated incidents rising nationally for a fourth consecutive year — +8% to 139, nearly triple 2020 — and identifies no trans-specific provincial pattern for the jurisdiction.

Enforcement signals cut both ways: a June 2025 provincial directive places transgender inmates according to anatomical sex rather than gender identity, reversing prior practice and challenged by advocates as violating the provincial charter of rights; against that, a June 2024 human-rights tribunal ruling ordered damages against a bar that discriminated against a trans woman in hiring on gender-identity grounds — enforcement can favour trans complainants. No jurisdiction-specific anti-trans legislation, ordinance or incident series appears in the surviving sources; the national criminal law and human-rights framework apply, and the jurisdiction's largest city anchors one of the country's most established organised 2SLGBTQ+ communities.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Litigation flux: after a two-month trial, the province's superior court declared provisions of the Civil Code invalid because they violated the fundamental rights of trans, intersex and non-binary people (2021), the court of appeal largely upheld the decision (2024), and the rulings led to legislative reform of the Civil Code — a landmark outcome that reshaped the province's rules on sex designation and identity documents.

Parent-nation context: the national hate-crime release records 4,882 reported incidents in 2024 (+1% on 2023) with provincial rates ranging from 5.3 to 16.0 per 100,000 and eight provincial units stable or declining; it reports no jurisdiction-specific rate figure, supporting the national-parity assessment. A national NGO analysis of the same police data accompanies the picture.
rewrites.localsOnly:

Resident census data: 2021 census figures show a small share (0.14%) of adult residents — and 0.27% of those aged 15-34 — identify as transgender.

rewrites.summary:
For a trans visitor to Ontario the legal floor is neutral: no jurisdiction-specific anti-trans statute, policy or official hostility is on record; while two other provincial units have legislated restrictions on trans names, pronouns or care, Ontario's government has not. Criminal law and human-rights protection operate nationally and uniformly across the country, and the provincial human-rights code explicitly protects gender identity and gender expression in employment, housing, facilities and services, contracts and association membership — the formal protections a visiting trans person holds.

Risk signals are national, not local: the national police-reported hate-crime series (Statistics Canada, March 2026) shows gender-identity/expression-motivated incidents rising nationally — +8% to 139 in 2024, a fourth consecutive increase — without identifying a trans-specific pattern for the jurisdiction.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
National context: the national series behind the assessment records 4,882 reported hate crimes in 2024 (+1% on 2023) at a national rate of 12.1 per 100,000; the jurisdiction's rate of 16.0 is the highest provincial figure, above the national average — the only province-specific number pointing above it in the release, and reporting is influenced by awareness and community trust.

Neighbour-side context: the 2023 pronoun-policy wave saw two other provincial units legislate parental consent for under-16s' name and pronoun changes at school; in the same week this jurisdiction's education minister said parents 'must be fully involved and fully aware' of such decisions, and the jurisdiction did not adopt such legislation then — officials held the line, with teachers and school boards weighing 'exceptional circumstances' and potential harm to the child.
rewrites.localsOnly: Resident-facing: the provincial human-rights commission's policy text — the official provincial statement of gender-identity protections — defines gender identity as a person's internal and individual experience of gender and notes that a chosen name and pronoun are common ways of expressing gender. No resident discrimination data or local surveys specific to the jurisdiction appear in the surviving sources.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
The jurisdiction's top provincial hate-crime rate covers all motivations (race/ethnicity, religion and sexual orientation dominate) and is not a trans-specific measure; it should not be read as gender-identity risk by itself.

The Egale analysis page by an LGBTIQ+ organisation was not retrievable at fetch time and is carried via its claim note. No source covers border or airport screening procedures for entering travellers, passport or identity-document policy, marriage, or partner-travel with the jurisdiction; those remain unverified for this jurisdiction. The jurisdiction's non-adoption of parental-consent legislation was the position as of August 2023; no later change is sourced.
